section: Scotland: SQA Applications of Mathematics climb (National 5 and Higher)

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (National 5) start here: check and plan
lessons.intention: We are finding out which of the National 5 Applications of Mathematics topics are already secure and which to learn first, and making a plan.
criteria: I can try one exam question on each of the 10 National 5 topics.
I know which topics I will work on first, and why.
I know how each topic works: lesson, online practice, exam-style sheet, then mini papers.

steps.start: Talk about the goal: National 5 Applications of Mathematics, practical maths in real contexts (money, statistics, measurement, planning).
steps.teach: Read the "What the exam expects: SQA Applications of Mathematics" sheet together. Then do the National 5 check (online or on paper), with a calculator but no help: it is a map, not a test.
steps.practise: The "SQA Applications of Maths climb: National 5 check" sheet, or the online National 5 check.
steps.check: Mark the check together and fill in the "SQA Applications of Maths climb: National 5 tracker" sheet: the topics that lost marks go first, in climb order.

lessons.home: Look at the tracker together and agree a weekly time for online practice.
lessons.vocab: course, paper, marking, step, secure
lessons.understand: Why should every answer say what it means in the context?
lessons.lookFor: Says Applications questions are about real decisions, and the last mark is often for the decision with a reason.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (National 5) 1: Numeracy: rounding, estimating and calculating in context
lessons.intention: We are learning to round, estimate and carry out multi-step calculations in real contexts, and to check answers make sense.
criteria: I can round to decimal places and significant figures.
I can estimate to check a calculation.
I can work through a multi-step money problem.

steps.start: A shop till says 4 items at £2.95 cost £118. How can you tell at once it's wrong?
steps.teach: Estimate first (round to 1 significant figure), then calculate, then compare. For multi-step problems, write each step on its own line with what it finds. Round only at the end, and to what the question asks.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5 Applications) 1: Numeracy: rounding, estimating and calculating in context" sheet, marked one bullet a mark, then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to estimate 48.7 × 6.2, then calculate it and say if the answer is sensible.

lessons.home: Estimate the total at the supermarket before you reach the till.
lessons.vocab: round, estimate, significant figure, decimal place, multi-step
lessons.understand: Why estimate before you calculate?
lessons.lookFor: Says it catches calculator slips, because a wrong answer will be far from the estimate.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (National 5) 2: Finance: pay, deductions and budgets
lessons.intention: We are learning to work out gross pay (including overtime and commission), deductions and net pay, and to plan a budget.
criteria: I can work out pay with overtime and commission.
I can work out income tax from a given allowance and rate.
I can find net pay from a payslip.
I can balance a simple budget.

steps.start: Show a payslip. What's the difference between gross pay and net pay?
steps.teach: Gross pay = basic + overtime (time and a half is 1.5 × the hourly rate) + commission (a percentage of sales, often above a threshold). Deductions: income tax on pay above the personal allowance, National Insurance and pension. Net = gross − deductions. A budget lists income and spending; what's left can be saved.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5 Applications) 2: Finance: pay, deductions and budgets" sheet, marked one bullet a mark, then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to work out the net pay from a made-up payslip with three deductions.

lessons.home: Look at a real payslip or bill together (with permission) and name each line.
lessons.vocab: gross pay, net pay, overtime, commission, income tax, National Insurance, personal allowance, budget
lessons.understand: Why is the tax rate applied only to income above the personal allowance?
lessons.lookFor: Says the allowance is tax-free, so only the part above it is taxed.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (National 5) 3: Finance: best deals, exchange rates, saving and borrowing
lessons.intention: We are learning to compare deals, change currency, and work out interest, depreciation and the cost of borrowing.
criteria: I can compare deals and say which is better value, with a reason.
I can convert currency, including commission.
I can work out simple and compound interest and depreciation.
I can find the total cost of a loan.

steps.start: Two phone contracts: £20 a month, or £100 up front and £15 a month. Which is cheaper?
steps.teach: Compare deals on the same basis (the same time or quantity) and finish with a decision and a reason. Exchange: take off commission first, then multiply by the rate. Compound interest: multiply by (1 + r) once a year. Depreciation: multiply by (1 − r). Cost of a loan: total repaid − amount borrowed.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5 Applications) 3: Finance: best deals, exchange rates, saving and borrowing" sheet, marked one bullet a mark, then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to compare two contracts over 24 months and state which is cheaper and by how much.

lessons.home: Find two deals on the same thing online and work out which is better value.
lessons.vocab: best value, exchange rate, commission, compound interest, depreciation, loan
lessons.understand: Why must a 'which is cheaper' answer include both totals?
lessons.lookFor: Says the decision mark needs a reason that comes from the working, and the totals are that reason.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (National 5) 4: Statistics: averages, spread and comparing data sets
lessons.intention: We are learning to calculate averages and measures of spread, including the standard deviation, and to compare two data sets in context.
criteria: I can find the mean, median and interquartile range.
I can calculate a standard deviation.
I can compare two data sets with one comment on average and one on spread.

steps.start: Two bus routes average 20 minutes. Which would you rather take, if one varies a lot more?
steps.teach: Averages say what's typical; spread (range, interquartile range, standard deviation) says how consistent. A comparison needs two sentences in context: one on the average, one on the spread (smaller spread = more consistent).
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5 Applications) 4: Statistics: averages, spread and comparing data sets" sheet, marked one bullet a mark, then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to compare two sets of times with one comment on average and one on consistency.

lessons.home: Time the same journey for a week and work out the mean and range.
lessons.vocab: mean, median, quartile, interquartile range, standard deviation, consistent
lessons.understand: Why does a comparison need a comment on spread as well as the average?
lessons.lookFor: Says two sets can have the same average but very different consistency.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (National 5) 5: Scattergraphs, probability and expected frequency
lessons.intention: We are learning to describe correlation, use a line of best fit, and work out probabilities and expected frequencies.
criteria: I can describe correlation on a scattergraph.
I can use a line of best fit to estimate.
I can find a probability and an expected frequency.

steps.start: Does more revision mean a higher mark? How could you show it?
steps.teach: Correlation: positive, negative or none. A line of best fit goes through the middle of the points; use it to estimate within the data. Probability = favourable ÷ total; expected frequency = probability × number of trials.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5 Applications) 5: Scattergraphs, probability and expected frequency" sheet, marked one bullet a mark, then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to estimate a value from a line of best fit and say how many times to expect an outcome in 60 trials.

lessons.home: Roll a dice 60 times and compare the results with what you'd expect.
lessons.vocab: correlation, line of best fit, probability, expected frequency, relative frequency
lessons.understand: Why is a prediction from a line of best fit only an estimate?
lessons.lookFor: Says the points don't lie exactly on the line, so real values vary around it.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (National 5) 6: Geometry: Pythagoras, gradient and area
lessons.intention: We are learning to use Pythagoras, gradient and area in practical problems.
criteria: I can use Pythagoras to find a missing side in context.
I can work out a gradient and compare it with a limit.
I can find the area of composite shapes.

steps.start: A ladder leans against a wall. What do you need to know to find how high it reaches?
steps.teach: Pythagoras: the longest side squared equals the sum of the other two squared. Gradient = vertical ÷ horizontal, in the same units; compare it with any limit and say if it's acceptable. Composite areas: split into rectangles, triangles and circles, then add or subtract.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5 Applications) 6: Geometry: Pythagoras, gradient and area" sheet, marked one bullet a mark, then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to check if a ramp rising 30 cm over 4 m meets a 1/12 rule.

lessons.home: Measure a ramp or slope near you and work out its gradient.
lessons.vocab: Pythagoras, hypotenuse, gradient, composite shape, area
lessons.understand: Why must rise and run be in the same units?
lessons.lookFor: Says gradient is a ratio, so mixing cm and m gives the wrong value.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (National 5) 7: Measurement: volume, surface area and packing
lessons.intention: We are learning to work out volumes and surface areas, and how many boxes fit in a container.
criteria: I can find the volume of prisms, cylinders, cones and spheres.
I can find a surface area.
I can work out how many boxes fit in a container.

steps.start: How many shoeboxes would fit in a car boot? How could you find out without trying?
steps.teach: Volume formulas: prism = area of cross-section × length; cylinder πr²h; cone ⅓πr²h; sphere ⁴⁄₃πr³. Packing: divide each dimension of the container by the box's, round down, then multiply.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5 Applications) 7: Measurement: volume, surface area and packing" sheet, marked one bullet a mark, then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them how many 10 cm × 8 cm × 5 cm boxes fit in a 45 cm × 30 cm × 22 cm container.

lessons.home: Measure a cereal box and a kitchen cupboard: how many boxes fit?
lessons.vocab: volume, surface area, prism, cylinder, cone, sphere, packing
lessons.understand: Why do you round down when packing?
lessons.lookFor: Says a part of a box can't be packed, so only whole boxes count.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (National 5) 8: Scale drawings, bearings and navigation
lessons.intention: We are learning to use scales and three-figure bearings, including back bearings, to plan routes.
criteria: I can use a map scale both ways.
I can measure and use three-figure bearings.
I can find a back bearing.

steps.start: On a 1 : 25 000 map, how far is 4 cm in real life?
steps.teach: Scale: real = map × scale factor (then change units). Bearings are measured clockwise from north, with three figures. The back bearing is the bearing ± 180°.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5 Applications) 8: Scale drawings, bearings and navigation" sheet, marked one bullet a mark, then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the real distance for 6.5 cm on a 1 : 50 000 map and the back bearing of 070°.

lessons.home: Plan a walk on an OS map and write the bearings for each leg.
lessons.vocab: scale, scale factor, bearing, three-figure bearing, back bearing
lessons.understand: Why do bearings use three figures?
lessons.lookFor: Says it avoids confusion, so 045° can't be misread as 45 or 450.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (National 5) 9: Time, speed, time zones and planning tasks
lessons.intention: We are learning to work with time, speed and time zones, and to find the shortest time for a set of tasks.
criteria: I can work out durations with the 24-hour clock.
I can use speed, distance and time.
I can adjust times for time zones.
I can find the shortest time for tasks that can overlap.

steps.start: A flight leaves at 22:30 and takes 9 hours. The destination is 5 hours behind. When does it land?
steps.teach: Durations: count up to the next hour. D = S × T, and convert minutes to hours. Time zones: find the time at home, then add if the place is ahead, take away if behind. Tasks: list which must follow which; tasks that can happen together take the longest of them.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5 Applications) 9: Time, speed, time zones and planning tasks" sheet, marked one bullet a mark, then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to plan a meal of four tasks and find the shortest time.

lessons.home: Plan a real day trip with departure times and journey times.
lessons.vocab: 24-hour clock, duration, speed, time zone, precedence
lessons.understand: Why do tasks that happen at the same time only count once?
lessons.lookFor: Says they run side by side, so only the longer one adds to the total time.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (National 5) 10: Tolerance, tariffs, flowcharts and reading charts
lessons.intention: We are learning to use tolerance, read tariffs and tables, and follow flowcharts.
criteria: I can find the range allowed by a tolerance.
I can decide if a measurement is acceptable.
I can work out a bill from a tariff.
I can follow a flowchart.

steps.start: A bag of crisps says 25 g ± 1 g. Is a 23.5 g bag acceptable?
steps.teach: Tolerance: m ± t means from m − t to m + t; inside is acceptable. Tariffs: fixed charges (per day or month) plus a rate per unit; change pence to pounds at the end. Flowcharts: follow each decision box exactly.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (National 5 Applications) 10: Tolerance, tariffs, flowcharts and reading charts" sheet, marked one bullet a mark, then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find an electricity bill from a standing charge and a unit rate.

lessons.home: Look at a real energy bill and find the standing charge and unit rate.
lessons.vocab: tolerance, tariff, standing charge, unit rate, flowchart
lessons.understand: Why does a tolerance have two limits?
lessons.lookFor: Says a part can be too small or too large, so both ends matter.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb: mini papers (National 5)
lessons.intention: We are practising exam questions from all the topics together, under exam conditions, and using the results to plan what to revise.
criteria: I can answer mixed questions without being told the topic.
I show my working and say what each answer means.
I can use my marks to choose which topics to go back to.

steps.start: Recap the habits: read twice, one step a line, money to two decimal places, and a decision with a reason.
steps.teach: Set up exam conditions: 20 to 25 minutes, quiet, calculator allowed. Do the questions you can first.
steps.practise: The "Mini paper: mixed questions (National 5 Applications)" or "Mini paper: longer questions (National 5 Applications)" sheet. Each print is a new paper.
steps.check: Mark it together one bullet a mark, then write the score and the topics to go back to on the tracker.

lessons.home: Redo the questions that lost marks, then the online mixed exam questions.
lessons.vocab: exam conditions, marking, topic, revise
lessons.understand: Your mini paper shows you lost marks on two topics. What do you do next?
lessons.lookFor: Goes back to those topics' lessons or exam sheets before the next mini paper.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (Higher) start here: check and plan
lessons.intention: We are finding out which of the Higher Applications of Mathematics topics are already secure and which to learn first, and making a plan.
criteria: I can try one exam question on each of the 7 Higher topics.
I know which topics I will work on first, and why.
I know how each topic works: lesson, online practice, exam-style sheet, then mini papers.

steps.start: Talk about the goal: Higher Applications of Mathematics, which builds on National 5's finance and statistics and adds planning, modelling and a project.
steps.teach: Read the "What the exam expects: SQA Applications of Mathematics" sheet together. Then do the Higher check (online or on paper), with a calculator but no help: it is a map, not a test.
steps.practise: The "SQA Applications of Maths climb: Higher check" sheet, or the online Higher check.
steps.check: Mark the check together and fill in the "SQA Applications of Maths climb: Higher tracker" sheet: the topics that lost marks go first, in climb order.

lessons.home: Look at the tracker together and agree a weekly time for online practice.
lessons.vocab: course, paper, marking, step, secure
lessons.understand: Why should every answer say what it means in the context?
lessons.lookFor: Says Applications questions are about real decisions, and the last mark is often for the decision with a reason.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (Higher) 1: Finance: borrowing, loans and mortgages
lessons.intention: We are learning to work out the cost of borrowing and mortgage repayments, and to compare loans.
criteria: I can find the total repaid and the extra cost of a loan.
I can express the extra as a percentage.
I can work out a mortgage repayment from a rate per £1000.

steps.start: Two loans of £5000: one over 2 years, one over 5. Which costs more in total, and why?
steps.teach: Total repaid = monthly payment × number of months; extra = total − borrowed; as a percentage, ÷ borrowed × 100. Mortgages: borrowed = price − deposit; repayment = (borrowed ÷ 1000) × rate per £1000.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher Applications) 1: Finance: borrowing, loans and mortgages" sheet, marked one bullet a mark, then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them for the monthly repayment on a £180 000 flat with a 10% deposit at £5.20 per £1000.

lessons.home: Compare two real loan adverts: which costs more in total?
lessons.vocab: loan, APR, total repayable, mortgage, deposit, per £1000
lessons.understand: Why can a lower monthly payment cost more overall?
lessons.lookFor: Says it is spread over more months, so the total repaid can be higher.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (Higher) 2: Finance: saving, investing and inflation
lessons.intention: We are learning to compare savings with AER, and to understand inflation and pay in real terms.
criteria: I can use compound interest and depreciation.
I can work out an AER from a monthly rate.
I can apply inflation over several years.
I can say if pay has risen in real terms.

steps.start: Your pay rose 3% but prices rose 5%. Are you better off?
steps.teach: AER = (1 + monthly rate)¹² − 1. Inflation multiplies prices by (1 + i) each year. Real change = (pay multiplier ÷ price multiplier) − 1: negative means buying power fell.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher Applications) 2: Finance: saving, investing and inflation" sheet, marked one bullet a mark, then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to work out the real change when pay rises 4% and prices 6.8%.

lessons.home: Find the current inflation rate and a savings rate: is the money growing in real terms?
lessons.vocab: AER, compound interest, inflation, real terms, buying power
lessons.understand: Why compare savings with AER?
lessons.lookFor: Says accounts pay interest at different intervals; AER puts them all on a yearly basis.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (Higher) 3: Statistics: sampling, summaries and outliers
lessons.intention: We are learning to choose a sample, summarise data and spot outliers.
criteria: I can name and describe kinds of sample.
I can work out a stratified sample.
I can find mean and standard deviation from sums.
I can test for outliers.

steps.start: You want to know what a school of 900 thinks. Who would you ask?
steps.teach: Samples: simple random, systematic, stratified, quota, cluster, opportunity; say the bias each might have. Stratified: each group's share × sample size. Outliers: beyond 1.5 × IQR from the quartiles.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher Applications) 3: Statistics: sampling, summaries and outliers" sheet, marked one bullet a mark, then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to plan a stratified sample of 40 from three groups.

lessons.home: Design a short survey for your family or friends and say how you'd sample.
lessons.vocab: sample, bias, stratified, systematic, standard deviation, outlier
lessons.understand: Why might an opportunity sample be biased?
lessons.lookFor: Says it only includes people easy to reach, who may not represent everyone.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (Higher) 4: Correlation and linear regression
lessons.intention: We are learning to interpret correlation coefficients and use regression lines to make predictions.
criteria: I can describe correlation from r.
I can use a regression equation to predict.
I can say when a prediction is reliable.

steps.start: Ice cream sales and temperature: what would you expect a scattergraph to show?
steps.teach: r near 1 or −1 is strong; near 0 is weak. A regression line y = a + bx predicts y; within the data range (interpolation) it is reasonably reliable, outside it (extrapolation) it is not. Correlation is not causation.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher Applications) 4: Correlation and linear regression" sheet, marked one bullet a mark, then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to predict from y = 12 + 2.5x and say if it is reliable at x = 90 when the data ran from 10 to 40.

lessons.home: Collect paired data (height and arm span) and plot it.
lessons.vocab: correlation coefficient, regression line, interpolation, extrapolation, causation
lessons.understand: Why is extrapolation unreliable?
lessons.lookFor: Says we don't know the pattern continues outside the data we have.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (Higher) 5: Probability, conditional probability and expected value
lessons.intention: We are learning to use probability rules, conditional probability and expected value to make decisions.
criteria: I can use the addition rule.
I can test if events are independent.
I can find a conditional probability.
I can work out an expected value.

steps.start: A raffle ticket costs £2 and there's a 1 in 50 chance of winning £60. Is it worth it?
steps.teach: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). Independent if P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). P(A given B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B). Expected value = sum of outcome × probability, minus any cost.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher Applications) 5: Probability, conditional probability and expected value" sheet, marked one bullet a mark, then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the expected gain of a game and say if it is fair.

lessons.home: Work out the expected value of a real raffle or prize draw.
lessons.vocab: probability, independent, conditional, expected value, fair game
lessons.understand: What does a negative expected value mean?
lessons.lookFor: Says that on average, over many games, you lose money.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (Higher) 6: Planning and decision making: critical paths and float
lessons.intention: We are learning to plan projects with precedence tables, find the critical path and float.
criteria: I can draw a precedence network.
I can find the critical path and the shortest time.
I can find the float of an activity.

steps.start: Redecorating a room: which jobs must wait for others?
steps.teach: List activities with durations and what they depend on. Paths through the network: the longest is the critical path, and its length is the shortest project time. Float = how long a non-critical activity can be delayed without delaying the project.
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher Applications) 6: Planning and decision making: critical paths and float" sheet, marked one bullet a mark, then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find the critical path and one float in a five-activity project.

lessons.home: Plan a real job at home (cooking, decorating) as a network.
lessons.vocab: precedence, network, critical path, float, Gantt chart
lessons.understand: Why is the shortest project time the length of the longest path?
lessons.lookFor: Says every path must be finished, so the project can't end before its longest path does.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb (Higher) 7: Mathematical modelling: linear and exponential
lessons.intention: We are learning to build and use linear and exponential models, and to judge them.
criteria: I can use a linear model to find a value.
I can use an exponential growth or decay model.
I can find when a model passes a target.
I can comment on a model's limits.

steps.start: A town grows 4% a year. Will it double in 10 years?
steps.teach: Linear: y = a + bx (a fixed start, the same amount each step). Exponential: y = a × (1 + r)ⁿ (the same percentage each step). To find when it passes a target, work year by year (or use logs). Comment on assumptions: will the rate really stay the same?
steps.practise: The "Exam practice (Higher Applications) 7: Mathematical modelling: linear and exponential" sheet, marked one bullet a mark, then the online practice.
steps.check: Ask them to find when £2000 at 5% a year passes £3000, and one assumption the model makes.

lessons.home: Model a real cost (a phone plan, a taxi) and check it against a bill.
lessons.vocab: model, linear, exponential, growth rate, assumption
lessons.understand: When is an exponential model better than a linear one?
lessons.lookFor: Says when it changes by the same percentage each time rather than the same amount.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb: mini papers (Higher)
lessons.intention: We are practising exam questions from all the topics together, under exam conditions, and using the results to plan what to revise.
criteria: I can answer mixed questions without being told the topic.
I show my working and say what each answer means.
I can use my marks to choose which topics to go back to.

steps.start: Recap the habits: read twice, one step a line, money to two decimal places, and a decision with a reason.
steps.teach: Set up exam conditions: 20 to 25 minutes, quiet, calculator allowed. Do the questions you can first.
steps.practise: The "Mini paper: mixed questions (Higher Applications)" or "Mini paper: longer questions (Higher Applications)" sheet. Each print is a new paper.
steps.check: Mark it together one bullet a mark, then write the score and the topics to go back to on the tracker.

lessons.home: Redo the questions that lost marks, then the online mixed exam questions.
lessons.vocab: exam conditions, marking, topic, revise
lessons.understand: Your mini paper shows you lost marks on two topics. What do you do next?
lessons.lookFor: Goes back to those topics' lessons or exam sheets before the next mini paper.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb: what the exam expects
lessons.intention: We are learning how Applications of Mathematics is examined and marked: the papers, the Higher project, step marks and decisions with reasons.
criteria: I know the papers for National 5 and Higher.
I know marks are given one step at a time.
I know a decision needs a reason from my working.

steps.start: Show an answer that says only 'Contract A'. How many marks should it get?
steps.teach: Go through the "What the exam expects: SQA Applications of Mathematics" sheet and mark its model answers together.
steps.practise: Mark the model answers on the "What the exam expects: SQA Applications of Mathematics" sheet together, then the online mixed exam questions.
steps.check: Ask them what a decision question needs for full marks.

lessons.home: Find SQA's specimen paper for the course and look at its first page.
lessons.vocab: paper, project, step mark, decision, context
lessons.understand: Why does the working matter even when the answer is right?
lessons.lookFor: Says marks are for each step, and the reason for a decision comes from the working.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: SQA Applications of Maths climb: my next step (working on your own)
lessons.intention: We are learning to follow the climb on our own: take the check, practise the next topic, mark our own work and know when to move on.
criteria: I can open the climb page and follow My next step.
I read the marking after every question.
I know when a topic is secure and when to move on.

steps.start: Ask: when you study on your own, how do you decide what to do next?
steps.teach: Open popspell.com/climb.html?course=apps together. Show My next step: the check first, then the first topic that needs work, then a mini paper when a stage is nearly done. Progress stays on this device only.
steps.practise: The "SQA Applications of Maths climb: my route through National 5 and Higher" sheet, then one practice set on the climb page.
steps.check: Ask them to show their next step and explain why that topic comes next.

lessons.home: Three sessions a week on the climb page, about 45 minutes each.
lessons.vocab: self-guided, marking, secure, next step
lessons.understand: Why read the marking even when you got the answer right?
lessons.lookFor: Says it shows which steps earn marks, so you can write them in the exam.
